claims.text: Mechanical alloying produces a nanocrystalline BCC solid-solution MgAlTiVFeCo precursor.
The initial sintered alloy has a homogeneous solid-solution structure with minimal surface oxide formation.
Processing MgAlTiVFeCo at about 1000 °C causes Al/Fe surface enrichment and forms a continuous spinel-type oxide film.
MgAlTiVFeCo specimens have been electrochemically tested in 3.5 wt% NaCl after sintering at 850–1000 °C.
A dense, continuous spinel-type oxide enriched in Al and Fe is the structural mediator of the tribo-corrosion response.
The oxide film provides a hard, low-friction surface that reduces mechanical wear.
The oxide film limits ion penetration and changes corrosion from direct attack to a diffusion-controlled process.
The oxide film regenerates after it is mechanically removed during sliding.
Competition between film removal and self-healing governs the total tribo-corrosion degradation rate.
The 1000 °C specimen has substantially greater passive-film resistance than specimens sintered at 850–950 °C.
The 1000 °C specimen has lower corrosion current density than the lower-temperature specimens.
High-temperature processing will reduce combined wear-plus-corrosion degradation relative to the lower-temperature baseline.
Film-removal events may transiently increase the wear component even though total degradation decreases.
Specimens sintered at 850–950 °C have a less developed or discontinuous oxide film and corrode by direct attack.
The lower-temperature specimens exhibit higher degradation than the 1000 °C specimen.
The predicted benefit holds when oxide-film regrowth is faster than mechanical removal.
The predicted benefit may fail at high mechanical removal rates or in environments that inhibit oxide formation.
Film-removal and regrowth kinetics during simultaneous wear and corrosion are not well quantified.
Failure of the 1000 °C specimen to show lower combined degradation, or failure of its film to recover after wear, would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.

contradictions.description: The conditions state that wear rate is kept constant, whereas the prediction treats the wear component as changing and the experiment measures wear rate as an outcome. Controlled sliding parameters could be held constant, but wear rate itself cannot simultaneously be fixed and used as a response variable.
